Let \(a=v_p(x), b=v_p(y), c=v_p(z)\). The divisibility conditions give
\[
a\le 3b,\quad b\le 3c,\quad c\le 3a.
\]
Let \(m=\min(a,b,c)\). By cyclic symmetry, assume \(m=a\). Then
\[
c\le 3a=3m,\qquad b\le 3c\le 9m,
\]
so
\[
a+b+c\le m+3m+9m=13m.
\]
By the ultrametric inequality,
\[
v_p(x+y+z)\ge \min(a,b,c)=m.
\]
Thus
\[
v_p(xyz)=a+b+c\le 13m\le 13v_p(x+y+z),
\]
so \(xyz\mid (x+y+z)^{13}\). Hence \(n=13\) works.

For necessity, take
\[
x=2,\quad y=2^9,\quad z=2^3.
\]
Then \(x\mid y^3\), \(y\mid z^3\), and \(z\mid x^3\). Also
\[
x+y+z=2+512+8=522=2\cdot 261,
\]
so \(v_2(x+y+z)=1\), while
\[
xyz=2^{13}.
\]
For \(xyz\mid (x+y+z)^n\), we need \(13\le n\). Therefore the smallest possible \(n\) is
\[
\boxed{13}.
\]
